blocks: In the POSIX sense, a directory is a special file whose content is a sequence of directory entries (struct dirent), each mapping a name to an OS/File/System/Inode number within the same file system.
The directory does not store file content or most metadata — those live in the inode. It is purely a name-to-inode mapping.
Every directory contains two automatic OS/File/System/Link/Hards: . (pointing to itself) and .. (pointing to the parent directory).
In everyday use, "directory" and "folder" are synonyms for a container that organizes files.
In the POSIX data-structure sense, a directory is the mechanism that gives a file its name: the name lives in the directory entry, not in the file itself.
An inode (index node) is the data structure in a Unix-like file system that stores a file's metadata and data-block pointers.
Each inode has a unique number within its file system. The OS/File/System/Directory stores the mapping from names to inode numbers; the inode itself does not store the filename.
File type (regular file, directory, symlink, device, …)
Timestamps: atime (last access), mtime (last modification), ctime (last status change)
Link count — the number of OS/File/System/Link/Hards pointing to this inode
Pointers to the data blocks that hold the file's content

The filename — that lives in the OS/File/System/Directory entry
What an inode does not store
The full path — a file can be reached by multiple paths if multiple hard links exist

The file's data is freed only when the link count reaches zero and no process holds the file open.
Hard links share one inode; each new hard link increments the link count.
A file system link is a name or pointer that lets one file-system location refer to file content or to another path.
The POSIX-core forms are OS/File/System/Link/Hard and OS/File/System/Link/Soft.
The conceptual overview is OS/File/System/Link/Concept/Comparison of Different Types.
Different Types of File System Links
Different Types of File System Links
POSIX-style file-system links let one file-system location reach content through more than one name, but the main link types do this in different ways.
Different Types of File System Links
A OS/File/System/Link/Hard is a direct name-to-OS/File/System/Inode mapping: the name is the file object. No path resolution happens; the OS reaches the file directly by inode number.
Different Types of File System Links

A OS/File/System/Link/Soft stores a path string as its payload. Each time it is followed, the OS walks the OS/File/System/Directory tree to resolve that string. If the target has moved or been deleted, the stored string leads nowhere — the link is dangling.
Different Types of File System Links
The practical difference: hard links cannot go stale because there is no path to become wrong; symlinks can go stale because the stored path may stop resolving.
Different Types of File System Links
Different Types of File System Links
File systems separate several ideas that are easy to blur together: bytes on storage, file metadata, directory entries, and pathnames. Links are where those layers become visible.
Different Types of File System Links

A pathname such as notes/today.md is resolved by walking directory entries. A hard link adds another directory entry to the same file object; a symbolic link inserts a path-redirection step into that walk.
Different Types of File System Links

The POSIX core is only part of the wider landscape. Windows shortcuts, Windows junctions, macOS Finder aliases, bind mounts, and reflinks are adjacent mechanisms, but they are not the focus of this overview.

Object link vs path link - Hard links connect another name to the same file object; symbolic links connect one path to another path.
Different Types of File System Links
Equal name vs pointer - Hard-linked names are peers. A symbolic link is visibly a link that points elsewhere.
Different Types of File System Links
Lifetime follows the model - A hard-linked file survives until the final hard link is removed; a symbolic link can survive after its target path stops resolving.
